newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - De Silguy says EU stability pact to stay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - De Silguy says EU stability pact to stay.

text.p: European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Monday the drive to monetary union was irreversible and that there would be no going back on the EU's "stability pact" on budget deficit control.

De Silguy, attending an OECD meeting here, was responding to reporters' queries about the possibility of France's opposition Socialist party seeking fresh discussions on the stability pact if they won power after the second round of a parliamentary election next Sunday.

Fresh talks on the stability pact, which is designed to make sure countries keep their deficits under control in the years after they enter monetary union, is one of several issues the Socialists have said they want to take up on Europe.

"No-one is considering re-negotiating the stability and growth pact," de Silguy told a news conference during a two-day meeting of ministers from the 29 member countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
De Silguy declined to comment directly on the left's lead in the first round of the parliamentary election on Sunday.
The surprise swing to the left opens up the possibility of the Socialists, probably along with the Communists, taking power from the centre-right government.
But de Silguy made it clear he did not think a European Union government of "whatever political colour" would go back on the budgetary accord thrashed out in Dublin last December.
"No, absolutely not, countries will not go back on their decision (to endorse the pact)," De Silguy said.
French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said in a newspaper interview this month he would not feel bound by the accord if the left won control of the National Assembly.
He has placed four key conditions on a single currency, including early entry for Italy and Spain and an "economic government" as a counterweight to the European central bank.

Other party officials have talked of reviewing the Dublin stability pact. The Communist party flatly opposes the single currency and wants a new referendum but Jospin has said that the Socialist position would be the only one on Europe if the left came to power.
De Silguy said there was no question of wavering on monetary union or tampering with the Maastricht treaty which lays down the conditions for the euro's launch from January 1, 1999.
"The single currency is an irreversible phenomenon," he told reporters. "The (Maastricht) treaty will not be re-negotiated, there will be no new conditions," he added.

He said the economic climate already existed for a majority of the European Union's 15 countries to qualify for monetary union from the start. He did not say how many countries he had in mind or which countries he was referring to.
"The euro will be launched on January 1, 1999. We are now on the home straight. It is up to member states to continue their (economic) convergence efforts to qualify (to join)," he said.
But he told Reuters there was no need to rush into sensitive decisions on how the parities between currencies that eventually join the euro should be fixed at the time of its launch.
"The Commission has not made any proposals, it will do so at the appropriate time...We have to look at a certain number of questions, but I would say there should be no undue haste."

Asked at the news conference whether he was worried a left-wing French government might relax austerity measures introduced by the centre-right coalition, De Silguy said EU countries had no alternative but to keep finances in order.
The French franc, stocks and bonds reacted sharply on Monday to the left's surge in Sunday's first round but prices steadied as investors saw little scope for radical policy changes.
The Socialists have said they are committed to sound financial management and Jospin said on Sunday France needed bold policies that were nonetheless careful on public spending.
